solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: BBC made her broadcast in crash site

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: the three words supply all ten letters

explanation.surface: A woman's programme went out on the BBC from the scene of an accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crash' is slang for sleeping, so a crash site is where you sleep: a BEDCHAMBER.
explanation.definitionFit: To crash is informal for going to sleep, and a bedroom is the place where that happens.

clue.text: Consignment from food store close to Coventry vicar sent back

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is taken
something sent back travels the opposite way, so these letters are read right to left

blocks.note: a deli is a shop selling prepared food
the last letter of the city name
Rev, short for Reverend, the title of a vicar

explanation.surface: A parcel from a delicatessen near Coventry gets returned by a clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: A delivery is a batch of goods handed over, just as a consignment is a shipment of goods.

clue.text: Spirited meeting of mass by northern church

blocks.note: a sea of faces is a great mass of them
N is the abbreviation for northern
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A lively gathering after a Mass, held near a church in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' looks religious next to 'church', but it means a large quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: A seance is a gathering held to contact spirits of the dead, hence a meeting full of spirits.

clue.text: A revolutionary headed with assistant for city

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the following word is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
to head a group is to lead it
an aide is a helper

explanation.surface: A rebel leader and their helper set out for a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Adelaide is a real city, the capital of South Australia.

clue.text: Look in bogs for serious criminals from America

indicators.note: one word placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: fens are marshy wetlands
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone peers into marshes searching for dangerous American outlaws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bogs' is also British slang for toilets, which pulls the surface elsewhere; here it means marshes.
explanation.definitionFit: In US law a felony is a grave crime, so the people who commit one are felons.

clue.text: Pork pie stuffed with slice of mouldy fruit

indicators.note: something stuffed with a filling holds it inside
a slice is a thin piece, here just the first letter

blocks.note: rhyming slang: pork pie means lie
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A pork pie filled with a piece of rotten fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pork pie' is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie; a pork pie is also a British meat pastry, which is the surface's picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A lime is a green citrus fruit.

clue.text: Cost for tenor to put on outdoor event

indicators.note: the tenor is put on, or placed into, the cost, so it ends up inside

blocks.note: a fee is a charge or cost
T is the abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: The price charged for a singer to perform at an open-air gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A fete is a fair or garden party, usually held outside to raise funds.

clue.text: See to Daisy in an excited state? Steady on!

indicators.note: an excited state is agitated and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the three words supply all ten letters

explanation.surface: Someone told to calm an agitated Daisy says 'steady on'.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half plays the scene in which the soothing words would be said, so the whole clue reads as one situation.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations urging someone to slow down and take care.

clue.text: What a pupil might see with a deficient head?

definitions.text: What a pupil might see with a deficient head?

blocks.clueFragment: What a pupil might see with a deficient head?
blocks.note: surface reading: an eye's pupil seeing something odd, perhaps an injured head
setter's reading: a school short of a teacher brings in a stand-in, whom the pupil sees

explanation.surface: An eye's pupil peering at a malformed head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupil' suggests the eye; it is a schoolchild. When staff are lacking, a temporary teacher covers the class.
explanation.definitionFit: A supply teacher is a substitute brought in to cover for an absent member of a school's staff.

clue.text: Movement splinter group fails to get going

indicators.note: failing to get going means losing the start, so the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: a faction is a dissenting group within a larger one

explanation.surface: A breakaway political group cannot get its campaign started.
explanation.definitionFit: Action and movement both mean motion or activity, the state of doing something.

clue.text: Motorway policeman's order for a light jumper?

blocks.note: first meaning: the instruction a traffic officer gives a driver to stop at the roadside
second meaning: a sweater, which the British call a jumper

explanation.surface: A traffic cop flags down a lightweight vehicle that is speeding.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is British for a sweater; the surface suggests something that jumps or a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a police command to stop a vehicle and a knitted garment put on over the head.

clue.text: Take care of paying passenger properly

blocks.note: a taxi driver's fare is the passenger who pays
to do something well is to do it properly

explanation.surface: Look after a customer correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take care' reads as an instruction to look after someone; here it is the parting phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Take care' is said when parting, so it serves as a goodbye.

clue.text: Unopened spirits I'd ultimately store behind bars

indicators.note: something unopened is missing its opening, so the first letter is removed
ultimately points to the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: gins are spirits
taken as written
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Sealed bottles of liquor I would keep locked away.
explanation.definitionFit: Inside is slang for in prison, and behind bars means the same.

clue.text: She rounded up rough-coated hunting dogs

indicators.note: when things are up they are in disarray, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: the two words supply all ten letters

explanation.surface: A woman herded together a pack of shaggy hounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rounded up' reads as one phrase, but 'rounded' is part of the letters and 'up' alone signals the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A deerhound is a large Scottish breed with a wiry coat, bred to chase deer.

clue.text: Type noble head annoyed too much?

indicators.note: someone annoyed is ruffled or upset, so the letters are disturbed

blocks.note: the three words supply all thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A grand figure at the top is irritated by excessive behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Conduct beyond the pale is unacceptable, going past what is tolerated, so it is excessive.

clue.text: One who talks over a film one's watching?

definitions.text: One who talks over a film one's watching?

blocks.clueFragment: One who talks over a film one's watching?
blocks.note: surface reading: an annoying cinemagoer chatting through the movie
setter's reading: the voice heard over the pictures, telling the story to the audience

explanation.surface: A rude person who chatters through a film in the cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talks over' sounds like interrupting; it means speaking as a voiceover.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrator supplies the spoken commentary that accompanies a film's images.

clue.text: Some pasta git ate desirously in a stew?

indicators.note: some of the words means a part of their run of letters

blocks.note: runs from the end of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: A greedy oaf eagerly eats pasta out of a casserole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a stew' looks like food, keeping with pasta, but means worried.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a stew is an idiom for being anxious or flustered, which is agitated.

clue.text: Be partial to quiet spliff with lower drug content

indicators.note: a lower drug content means some drug is taken out, so a letter for it is removed

blocks.note: p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
a reefer is a cannabis cigarette
E is slang for ecstasy

explanation.surface: Fancy a calm, weaker joint.
explanation.walkthrough: A spliff is British slang for a cannabis joint.
explanation.definitionFit: To prefer something is to favour or like it more, which is being partial to it.

clue.text: Fellow delivering Whoppers in a plane?

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
whoppers are big lies, so telling them is lying

explanation.surface: A man bringing Burger King's Whopper burgers aboard a jet.
explanation.walkthrough: Whopper is a burger brand, steering toward food delivery; whoppers here are tall tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone flying is travelling by air, that is, in an aircraft.

clue.text: A large window framing river is just fine

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for large
a light is a pane or window
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A big window that looks onto a river is perfectly good.
explanation.definitionFit: All right means satisfactory or acceptable, the same as just fine.

clue.text: Drunk didn't go without drop of cognac

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, here just the first letter
without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: colours that clashed did not go together
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A drunkard abstained from even a sip of brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Didn't go' suggests staying home; it means failed to match. Lashed is British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Lashed is informal British slang for heavily intoxicated.

clue.text: Man of many parts my hot pal cast

indicators.note: to cast is to throw or mould anew, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: the three words supply all eight letters

explanation.surface: An actor of wide range, my attractive friend, is given roles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' and 'cast' suggest acting; the many parts are fields of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A polymath has expertise in many subjects, so is a person of many talents.

clue.text: Gemstone found in old china

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
rhyming slang: china plate means mate

explanation.surface: A precious stone discovered in antique porcelain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like porcelain; in Cockney rhyming slang it means a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is a milky iridescent gemstone.

clue.text: Stony figure, say, seen around university

indicators.note: one word seen around another wraps it

blocks.note: to state is to say
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A cold, expressionless person, for instance, spotted on campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example' but supplies the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A statue is a carved figure, often of stone.

clue.text: Perhaps heading at sea for Turkey with vegetables?

blocks.note: the main is a poetic name for the open sea
a ship's heading is its direction of travel

explanation.surface: A ship's bearing out at sea, perhaps, towards the country of Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: Turkey looks like the country; it is the bird served at dinner. The question mark marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Roast turkey with vegetables is a typical example of the principal dish of a meal.

clue.text: Having given British the slip, curls in goals

indicators.note: having given someone the slip, you have left them behind, so that letter is shed
giving someone the slip means escaping them, so that letter departs

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
bends are curves or curls

explanation.surface: A footballer's shots curl into the net after evading the British defence.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends are aims or objectives, which is what goals are.
